passage:
Dear Varun Chetta,
You asked on the phone why I sound so flat. I'll try to answer here, because writing is easier than saying it.
For about three months I've been waking at four with my heart racing, dreading school. I haven't told anyone, for a whole list of reasons. Achan says counsellors are for people who can't manage their own minds. I worry it costs a lot, and Amma is already counting every rupee. Mostly, I tell myself it isn't bad enough. I still go to class. I still smile in photos.
But a senior at school waited until she couldn't leave the house at all. I don't want to wait that long.
Our school counsellor is free. When you're home next Saturday, will you come with me, and help me tell Amma and Achan?
Gopika

qa.q: At what time has Gopika been waking up?
qa.a: At four, with a racing heart.

qa.q: Why has Gopika told nobody?
qa.a: Gopika is afraid Achan will see it as weakness, worries about the cost for Amma, and thinks it isn't bad enough.

qa.q: What choice does Gopika make at the end of the letter?
qa.a: To ask early: Gopika asks Varun Chetta to come to the free school counsellor and help tell Amma and Achan.

qa.q: How might Varun Chetta feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel worried but glad to be trusted, and able to make the first step less frightening for Gopika.

grounding: It shows a teenager held back by fear of seeming weak, cost, family reaction and feeling it is not bad enough, who decides to ask for help early.

passage: Jahnavi, since this podcast is about asking for help, here's why I waited so long. I'm Farida, and I kept a list of excuses. First: people would call me weak. In our class, anyone who cried was a joke for weeks. Second: my parents already work double shifts, and I thought a counsellor would cost money we didn't have. Third, the big one: it wasn't bad enough. Other people had real problems. So I waited. In Class 10 I stopped sleeping properly, then stopped reading, which I used to love, then stopped answering my friends. By the time I told our sports teacher, I'd missed a whole term. She listened, took me to the school counsellor that same afternoon, and it turned out the service was free. If I could talk to the Class 10 me, I'd say: the day you start making excuses is the day to ask.

qa.q: Whom did Farida finally tell?
qa.a: Farida's sports teacher.

qa.q: Why did Farida believe it "wasn't bad enough"?
qa.a: Farida felt unsure her struggle counted, since other people had real problems, so asking for help seemed unjustified.

qa.q: What did waiting cost Farida, and what choice would Farida make now?
qa.a: Farida missed a whole term; now Farida would ask for help as soon as the excuses start.

qa.q: How might the sports teacher have seen Farida's decision to speak up?
qa.a: The teacher would likely see it as brave and act quickly, taking Farida to the counsellor that same afternoon.

grounding: It shows a teenager who delayed asking for help out of fear of seeming weak, worry about cost and feeling it was not serious enough, and learned to ask early.

passage: In Lyon, Clara, fifteen, had been crying herself to sleep for two months. She hadn't told anyone. What if they called her weak? Her parents were already stressed; her father always said, "We don't air our problems." And anyway, other people had it worse. Her friend Camila found her in the library staring at nothing. "You've been sad for ages. Have you thought of talking to someone?" "It's not bad enough," Clara said. "You don't have to wait till it's bad enough," Camila said. "The school nurse is free, and she can help you find a counsellor. My cousin went. It was the bravest thing she did." That afternoon, Clara knocked on the nurse's door, heart racing.

qa.q: How long had Clara been crying herself to sleep?
qa.a: For two months.

qa.q: Why was Clara afraid to ask for help?
qa.a: She feared being called weak, worried about her parents' reaction and felt her struggle wasn't bad enough.

qa.q: What did Camila say that helped Clara ask early?
qa.a: That she didn't have to wait until it was bad enough, the school nurse was free and asking was brave.

qa.q: How might Camila have felt seeing Clara staring at nothing?
qa.a: Camila was probably concerned and caring, which is why she spoke up.

grounding: Shows a teenager held back from asking for help by fear of seeming weak, family reaction and thinking it's not bad enough, then asking early as a sign of strength.

passage: For the third time that week, Seema, sixteen, stood outside the school counsellor's door and didn't knock. Her mind listed reasons. It's not bad enough; I'm only sad, not sick. If Papa finds out, he'll say I'm bringing shame on the family. The girls will call me pagal if they see me here. She had been lying awake for weeks and her marks had slipped. She turned to leave. The door opened. Chandrika, the counsellor, smiled. "I've seen you here a few times. You're welcome to come in. You don't need to be at your worst to talk." Seema hesitated. "It's probably nothing." "Then let's talk about nothing for ten minutes." Seema went in. Later she wished she'd knocked the first day.

qa.q: How many times had Seema stood outside the door that week?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Seema afraid of?
qa.a: She feared her father's reaction, being called pagal by other girls and that her problems weren't bad enough.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say that lowered Seema's barriers?
qa.a: She welcomed Seema warmly and said she didn't need to be at her worst to talk, offering just ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt seeing Seema at the door again?
qa.a: She may have felt concerned and patient, gently opening the door to make asking easier.

grounding: Shows a teenager kept from asking by fear of being called weak, family reaction and feeling it isn't bad enough, and the relief of asking.

passage:
Dear Aparna didi,
I've tried to write this five times. I'm not okay, and I haven't been for months. I can't sleep, I've stopped going to football, and I keep feeling scared for no reason.
I didn't tell anyone because Papa says counselling is for weak people. And I know things are tight at home, so I thought getting help would cost too much. And I kept telling myself other people have real problems.
But you once told me you saw a counsellor in college and it helped. Can you help me find out if the school counsellor is free, or a helpline I can call? And maybe help me tell Mummy?
I think asking you is the bravest thing I've done this year.
Tushar

qa.q: What has Tushar stopped going to?
qa.a: Football.

qa.q: What made Tushar hesitate to ask for help?
qa.a: Tushar feared being seen as weak, worried about cost and the family's reaction, and thought the problem wasn't real enough.

qa.q: What does Tushar ask Aparna didi to help with?
qa.a: Finding out about a free school counsellor or helpline and helping Tushar tell Mummy.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Aparna may feel concerned and touched, and proud that Tushar trusted Aparna enough to ask.

grounding: Shows a teenager held back by fear of seeming weak, worries about cost and family reaction, and doubt that it's bad enough, choosing to ask as an act of strength.

passage:
So, Sarika, you asked why I didn't ask for help sooner. I'm Rashmi, Class 11, and honestly, I had a whole list of reasons.
One: people at school say only weak people go to the counsellor. Two: I thought it would cost money, and home was already tight. Three: I was scared of what Papa would say. "What will people think?" is his favourite line. Four, the big one: I kept telling myself it wasn't bad enough. Other people had real problems.
So I waited. For almost a year. I stopped sleeping, stopped drawing, cried in the washroom most days.
Then I finally knocked on the counsellor's door. Turns out it's free at our school. She helped me talk to Papa, and he actually listened.
If you're waiting until it's bad enough, don't. Going early wasn't weak. It was the bravest thing I've done.

qa.q: How long did Rashmi wait before asking for help?
qa.a: Almost a year.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling while putting off asking for help?
qa.a: Rashmi felt afraid of looking weak and of Papa's reaction, anxious about cost, and unsure the problem was bad enough.

qa.q: What would you advise someone with the same list of reasons?
qa.a: Ask early, since services like the school counsellor may be free and can even help with family talks; waiting only lets things get worse.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when the counsellor helped Rashmi talk to him?
qa.a: He might have been surprised and worried at first, then caring, since he actually listened.

grounding: Rashmi fears being called weak, worries about cost and family reaction and thinks it isn't bad enough, waits too long, then learns asking early is strength.
